summary: This document describes the Diameter application used for authentication, authorization, and accounting in the Network Access Server environment. It obsoletes RFC 4005 and is used together with the Diameter Base protocol, Transport Profile, and EAP specifications.

eli5.summary: When you plug into a network, a gatekeeper must check who you are, what you may do, and what you used. This is how the gatekeeper talks to the record keeper.

what is a network access server
what is an aa-request in diameter
subtitle: How a network access server asks a Diameter server who may connect, what they may do, and what they used.

tldr.problem: A network access server (NAS) that lets users dial in or plug in needs a central server to check identities, decide what each user may do, and record usage.
tldr.mechanism: The NAS sends AA-Request messages to a Diameter server and gets AA-Answers carrying authorization AVPs. Session-Termination, Abort-Session and Accounting messages cover the rest of the session.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7155 replaces RFC 4005, is not backward compatible with it, and drops the old RADIUS/Diameter interaction material.

today: RFC 7155 is a Standards Track document that obsoletes RFC 4005, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the current definition of the Diameter NAS application in this archive.

sections.title: What the NAS Application Is
sections.content:
RFC 7155 describes the Diameter application used for Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) in the Network Access Server (NAS) environment. A NAS is a device that provides an access service for a user to a network. The service may be a network connection or a value-added service such as terminal emulation.

On its own the document is not enough. Combined with the Diameter Base protocol (RFC 6733), the Transport Profile (RFC 3539) and the EAP application (RFC 4072), it satisfies the NAS-related requirements of RFC 2989 and RFC 3169.

A node that conforms to this specification advertises it by including the value 1 in the Auth-Application-Id of its Capabilities-Exchange-Request. The same value is used in the AA-Request, Re-Auth-Request, Session-Termination-Request and Abort-Session-Request messages.
sections.eli5: A NAS is a doorman for a network. This document is the script the doorman uses when calling the central office to ask whether to let someone in.

sections.title: Calls, Ports and Sessions
sections.content:
A new call or service connection arriving at a NAS port starts the exchange. The NAS packages information about the call, the user's identity and the user's authentication information into an AA-Request (AAR) and sends it to a server. The server replies with an AA-Answer (AAA) carrying authorization information or a failure in the Result-Code AVP.

If the Result-Code is DIAMETER_MULTI_ROUND_AUTH, more authentication is needed, and several AAR and AAA messages may follow until the transaction finishes. When it succeeds, the NAS application SHOULD start a session context.

Reauthentication reuses the original Session-Id. The server tells the NAS the maximum time allowed through the Authorization-Lifetime AVP, and the NAS MUST reauthenticate or reauthorize at the end of that period. A server can also push a Re-Auth-Request (RAR), which the NAS MUST answer with a Re-Auth-Answer (RAA). A failed reauthentication ends the service.

On termination, the NAS MUST send a Session-Termination-Request (STR) so the server can free resources. A NAS that receives an Abort-Session-Request (ASR) for an active session MUST answer with an Abort-Session-Answer (ASA) and disconnect the PPP or tunneling session.
sections.eli5: The doorman phones the office with your name. The office may say 'ask one more question', and the doorman asks you. Later the office can call back to say 'check again' or 'send them out'.

sections.title: The Ten Commands
sections.content:
The application defines five request and answer pairs. Each pair shares a command code, and the request has the 'R' bit set in the Command Flags field. All messages use the standard Diameter Command Code Format.

  • AAR/AAA (265): request and answer for authentication and/or authorization. The Auth-Request-Type AVP says which; the recommended value for most situations is AUTHORIZE_AUTHENTICATE.
  • RAR/RAA (258): the server asks the NAS to reauthenticate or reauthorize a session, for example to confirm that a prepaid user is still online.
  • STR/STA (275): the NAS reports that a session is ending, and the server releases its resources.
  • ASR/ASA (274): a server asks the NAS to stop a session. The answer uses DIAMETER_SUCCESS, DIAMETER_UNKNOWN_SESSION_ID if the session is not active, or DIAMETER_UNABLE_TO_COMPLY otherwise.
  • ACR/ACA (271): accounting reports from the NAS and their acknowledgements.

For a multi-round exchange, the follow-up AAR SHOULD carry the user's response in a User-Password AVP and MUST include any State AVPs from the previous answer. If a Reply-Message prompt cannot be delivered to the user, the NAS MUST treat the answer as an error and deny access.
sections.eli5: There are five kinds of phone call between doorman and office: let them in, check again, they left, send them away, and here is the bill. Each call has a question and a reply.

sections.title: AVPs by Purpose
sections.content:
Diameter messages carry data in AVPs (attribute-value pairs). This RFC groups the NAS-specific ones by purpose: session identification, authentication, authorization, tunneling and accounting. AVP Codes 0 to 255 are reserved for RADIUS attributes carried over into Diameter, and where an AVP derives from a RADIUS attribute, the range and format of its values are kept for easier transition.

Session AVPs describe the call, such as NAS-Port, Called-Station-Id and Calling-Station-Id. Authentication AVPs carry passwords or challenge responses, for example User-Password (limited to 128 bytes before encryption) and the CHAP-Auth group.

Authorization AVPs describe what the user gets. The Service-Type AVP SHOULD be present in all messages and decides which others apply: Login (1), Framed (2), Callback Login (3) or Callback Framed (4). Framed access covers items such as Framed-IP-Address, Framed-Route, Framed-Pool and Framed-MTU, whose value MUST be in the range 64 to 65535. A request may include hints, and the server is not required to honor them.

The Tunneling grouped AVP (code 401) describes a compulsory tunnel and requires the Tunnel-Type, Tunnel-Medium-Type, Tunnel-Client-Endpoint and Tunnel-Server-Endpoint AVPs. The RFC also defines the QoSFilterRule format for marking or metering traffic, but the QoS-Filter-Rule AVP is NOT RECOMMENDED in favor of the AVPs of RFC 5777.

Section 5 closes the section with AVP occurrence tables showing how many times each AVP may appear in each message.
sections.eli5: An AVP is a labeled sticky note on the phone call, like 'name: Sam' or 'speed limit: slow'. The notes are sorted into piles by what they are for.

sections.title: Accounting
sections.content:
If accounting is active, Accounting-Request messages SHOULD be sent after each authentication or authorization transaction and at the end of a session. The Accounting-Record-Type AVP says what kind of event it is. The first successful transaction SHOULD cause a START_RECORD, later ones an INTERIM_RECORD. For a given session there MUST be only one matching START and STOP pair with any number of INTERIM records between them, or a single EVENT_RECORD saying why a session did not start.

Accounting AVPs include Accounting-Input-Octets, Accounting-Output-Octets, the matching packet counters, and Acct-Session-Time in seconds. These counters can only appear in INTERIM or STOP records. Acct-Delay-Time tells the server how many seconds the client has been trying to send a record, so the server can estimate when the event happened.

It is RECOMMENDED that the coupled accounting model of RFC 6733 be used, so the Acct-Application-Id AVP in the accounting messages SHOULD be set to 1.
sections.eli5: The record keeper writes down when you arrived, how much you used while you were there, and when you left, one entry for each.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Use of this application MUST take into account the security requirements of the Base protocol. The document contains no security protocol of its own, but it discusses how the PPP authentication protocols PAP and CHAP are carried inside Diameter.

PAP SHOULD be discouraged because it exposes passwords to possibly untrusted entities, although it is also used with one-time passwords, which are not a risk. CHAP is carried for RADIUS backward compatibility, and as used in a RADIUS environment it facilitates authentication replay attacks. EAP can offer better security with a suitable method.

Almost every AVP defined here is security-sensitive. Only Configuration-Token, QoS-Filter-Rule and Tunneling are not. Messages with sensitive AVPs MUST be sent only over mutually authenticated TLS or IPsec, and MUST NOT pass through intermediate nodes unless there is end-to-end security or locally trusted configuration saying it is not needed. The document specifies no end-to-end mechanism.

An authorization-only request carries no authentication, so a new session cannot safely be started from the response to one without introducing a significant security vulnerability.
sections.eli5: Passwords are secrets, so the phone line between doorman and office has to be private. Some old ways of proving who you are can be copied by a sneaky listener, so better ways are preferred.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 4005
sections.content:
RFC 7155 obsoletes RFC 4005 and is not backward compatible with it. The main changes:

  • All material about RADIUS/Diameter protocol interactions was removed.
  • The Accounting-Request and Accounting-Answer formats now explicitly require the Acct-Application-Id AVP and exclude the Vendor-Specific-Application-Id AVP. The RFC argues the semantics are unchanged, because RFC 4005 already required an Acct-Application-Id.
  • Lists of RADIUS attribute values were replaced by references to the IANA registries.
  • The accounting model is now specified (see the Accounting section).

Errata filed against RFC 4005 at the time of writing were reviewed and incorporated as necessary.
sections.eli5: This is a rewrite of an older rulebook. It cleans things up, but old devices following the old rulebook may not match the new one exactly.
